utterances.text: It was not so clear in the transcript. I think the witness said something else. To the best of my recollection, he said that at that time there was no water in the city and the city water supply system was not in order, something like that. So maybe our friend can clarify that with the witness. Because this sentence: "... the city water supply system, but what we had to do ..." was not so -- is not so clear, and it's not in accordance with what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, just to step back to clear the record for us: You said that you had to bring water from the well. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Because the city water supply system was broken. There was no water in the bathroom or in the toilets.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I clarify now: Are there two persons, one named Slobodan Jakupovic and another one called Dadan Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No. There is only Dadan Jakupovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And did you hear that he had been killed while you were being detained in that first room?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: How did you hear he had been killed?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that morning, very early, around 5.00, a shot, and then later we found out from Mirsad Kirkic, who was in the hall - he was cleaning the hall - that it was Dadan that was shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Where was Dadan when he was shot?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: At that time he was at the Territorial Defence. As far as I know, from what I heard, he was at the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And at the time you heard the shot, did you have a look out the window that you indicated in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And does that window look across onto the TO building where you had -- where you understood Dadan was detained?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you see people standing outside the TO around the time of the shot?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Simo Zaric and the Red Berets, the so-called Kapetan Dragan Unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And did you see them react to the shot, or how did they behave when the shot sounded out?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I saw no reaction. They were just standing there and talking amongst themselves, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: After this day when you heard the shot and you learnt that Dadan had been killed, did you stay in that single room by yourself for much longer?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: How much longer did you stay in the single room?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe another couple of hours. I was transferred to another room at 10.00 at night, where there were 20 other people detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was that room just down the corridor from the room that you had been in by yourself?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, right next to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So it was also on the bottom floor of the SUP building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: These 20 or so other people, do you know the ethnic background of the people in the room?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber what they were -- what it was?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, was there anybody of Serb ethnicity detained in that room?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was everybody in that room dressed in civilian clothes or was anybody wearing a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: They were all in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, I'd first -- I want to cover a number of things that happened while you were detained in this room, and first I'd just like to touch on the general conditions. You said you hadn't received food since you had been detained. Did you get food in the second room?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do I understand that -- could you tell us what sort of food that was?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: In this other room, we started getting cooked food, cooked meals.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was it -- what were the portions like? Was it a lot of food or would you have to share food amongst all 20 of you? Could you just give us an idea of how often or what sort of food you had amongst the 20 of you in that room.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: In that room, every morning and every night we got one soldier's ration per four of us and one loaf of bread per five of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And the soldier's ration consisted of -- what was it? Kind of a porridge, a meal?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: It's the standard soldier's ration for soldiers in the field. Every soldier had a can that was filled by one standard meal.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you go to the toilet when you wanted from this second room?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you allowed to go to the toilet at appointed times or would you be guarded when you went to the toilet?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Always in the morning, escorted by the guards, one by one, after which we went straight back to the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you and the other 20 or so persons in that room subjected to beatings whilst you were detained there?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Would you be beaten in the room or would you be taken out for the beatings to be administered?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Mainly inside the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Who would come in to beat you? Would they be police officers, would they be people in military uniform, or would they be people in civilian uniform, or a mixture of all of those?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: People wearing military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Would they beat you with implements, or would they just beat you with their fists and legs?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: They mainly kicked us with -- kicked us and beat us with their fists and sometimes grabbed anything that was at hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did they ever force any detainees to hit each other or -- to hit each other?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you ever -- were you ever the victim of being hit by any of these people or another detainee, or were you ever forced to beat up on the other detainees by the people in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was hit by Mirsad Jasarevic, also known as Bjelko.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And Mirsad Jasarevic, was he forced to hit you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was forced to beat us, to slap us, more precisely. When he slapped you once, if you hadn't fallen to the ground, he would get hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was this particularly humiliating, being hit by one of your own, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: This Mirsad Jasarevic, also known as Bjelko, did you ever witness him being beaten by other people?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was beaten in the hallway outside our room, in precisely that section of the hallway.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mehinovic, I would like to get the details of this particular beating that you witnessed. So if you'll bear with me, I'll take you through it slowly. Was Mr. Jasarevic detained in the room with you, or was he detained somewhere else in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No. He was detained in the garage, and he had been brought on that occasion to the hallway.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And how did you know that he was being brought out of the garage to the hallway?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I knew from those men who did the sweeping and cleaning and who washed their cars. They would tell us who was being taken where.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: On this occasion, did you hear someone give orders that Mirsad Jasarevic should be brought up from the garages?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you say "Milan Simic," do you mean Milan Simic who you described earlier and said whose father you knew very well?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And you're sure that it was Milan Simic who asked for Mirsad to be brought up from the garages?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And how can you be so sure that it was Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Because the door was open, the hallway was lit, and the beating was watched by all of us who were inside. And after that, Mirsad was brought to our room to slap us.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: From the position you had in the room, could you actually see Milan Simic at some stage out in the corridor?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I was standing right next to the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And could you see when Mirsad Jasarevic was actually brought into the hallway?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I was sitting to the right of the door, which was ajar. I couldn't see the staircase. I only saw him when he entered the hallway together with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you see what Mirsad was being beaten with? Was he being punched, or was he being beaten with implements?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: With a truncheon. He was also being punched and kicked, and the truncheon was a police one.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you hear whether there were any insults or comments being made to Mirsad while he was being assaulted?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I was very close. It might have been a metre and a half away. There were insults. They were cursing his mother, his sister.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you consider these --

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just for clarification purposes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: -- he said "they" were cursing his mother. If we could just have clarification as to who "they" was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I appreciate Defence counsel's concern. I do intend to go back and clarify a number of those issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: First, Mr. Mehinovic, could you just clarify for us on the matter of the -- when you say "cursing his mother and sister," were these particularly, shall I say, racist cursings, referring to his ethnic background, or were they just general crude curses?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Just profanities.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned that they -- you know, that they were cursing him. Who was doing the cursing exactly?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: It was Lugar. The man was known as Lugar. I don't know either his first or last name. There was also Tihi; perhaps the duty officer Savo; we called him the man from Rijeka, although I'm not sure he was from Rijeka, but he hadn't lived in Samac before. So those were the four men.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And do I understand that Milan Simic who had order -- or that you heard ordered Mirsad be brought up from the garage was with the men you just named?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you see whether each of these persons were participating in the beating, or could you just see general -- the group beating Mirsad -- could you distinguish - if you understand what I mean by distinguish - each individual, or could you just see the general beating?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: As a group. Because one man would hit him, and he would stagger. And then he would stagger all the way to the -- to the next man. And they would -- he was actually bouncing among them like a ball.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And could you see Milan Simic participating in this group assault?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you see whether -- how badly Mirsad was injured from this assault?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I could. He was swollen so much that his eyes were closed, and his head was very swollen, and he was so exhausted that he could barely stand.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You testified that after this beating, he was brought into the room where you and 20 others were being held; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did Milan Simic or was it one of the other police officers accompany him into the room?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: They were standing at the door and in the hallway, and they would laugh at every blow dealt by Bjelko.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: But can I clarify. Who brought Mirsad Jasarevic into the room where you were detained after he was beaten in the hallway?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Milan told him -- because we could hear from the hallway when Lugar told him, "You will now beat them one by one. And if you don't fell the man that you hit, you will get beaten." And when he got to the door, Milan told him, "What are you waiting for? Get in."

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And can you then say what -- what did Mirsad do? He came into your room, and did he indeed have to beat up the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: He did. If he hadn't started to slap us, he would be beaten even more.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: After he'd finished beating you, was -- do you know whether Mirsad was returned to his cell, or was he left in your room?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: He remained in the lower part, in the farther part of the hallway, and he spent the night on the bare cement floor. And after that, in the morning, they took him back to the garage.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: How do you know that he spent the night on the cement floor you've just described?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: When we were taken to the lavatory in the morning, he was still lying there in the farthest section of the hallway.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you saw Milan Simic in the corridor and witnessed this assault, was Milan Simic wearing civilian clothes or was he dressed in a uniform?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: A uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you tell from your vantage point whether or not he was also carrying a weapon?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I could. He also had a pistol, but I don't know the type.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was that the only time that you --

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Baen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: The witness said that Milan Simic was wearing a uniform. If he could clarify what type of uniform. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I trust you understood the question, Mr. Mehinovic. The uniform that Mr. Milan Simic was wearing, could you tell us the type of uniform it was?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: A camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this the only time that you personally witnessed Milan Simic beating up one of the detainees in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, how long did you spend, if you can estimate for us, in this second room where there were 20 or so of you? How long in total was your detention in that particular room?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps up to a month or just over a month. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: During your month there, were you ever asked to come out and clean the toilets or the hallways?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And on one occasion when you had to clean the toilets in the hallways, did you see any women being detained in the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you just briefly describe for us what you witnessed in terms of women being detained in the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: First I saw their faces. It was Behka Barjaktarevic. And I know the other one too. She was manager of a department store, married to a local man from Samac. I don't know her name. And while I was cleaning the hallway and before I got to the lavatory, Steven Todorovic and his favourite bodyguards, Goran, and Vukovic, Zvarka, Sole, and his team already were inside. And I heard screaming from that room, while two of the men were standing and laughing in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. You did mention before the break, in response to Her Honour's, question that one of the injuries you had sustained was a -- I believe you said fracture to your finger. Was that finger broken during your stay here in the month in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And was it deliberately broken by some of the people in authority working in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Stevan Todorovic asked me which hand I used for shooting, and he hit me with a rifle butt.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: During this -- one last question. The screaming you've described hearing from the room - I take you back now to when you were in the hallway doing your cleaning of the toilets - was that screaming of female or male voices?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Female.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, do you think we could clarify what was the name of the person that the witness refers to on page 55, line 25? In response to your question, he says: "First I saw their faces. It was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Behka ..." something or the other. Could we clarify who the people were, if he can?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, so that it's very clear on our record, could you again give us the names, if you know them, of the women you saw in the SUP building? Could you pronounce it very clearly so that the correct name could come out on the record?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: This first woman I know, and her name was Behka, B-e-h-k-a, Barjaktarevic. And I don't know the other one's last name. Her first name was Nihada. She was married to a man from Bosanski Samac and she is originally from Gradacac. Her name is Nihada, N-i-h-a-d-a. The first woman's last name is B-a-r-j-a-k-t-a-r-e-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's now clear for the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: During this month or so that you spent with the 20 other people in the room, did you get asked then to make this infamous statement you were originally asked to come to the SUP to give?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I hadn't given any statement there in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did anyone explain to you why you were being detained for a month and offer you any explanation to any charges or suspicion against you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you have any access to a doctor to treat any of your increasing medical wounds?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: At any stage were you told that you would be asked -- that you would be assigned a lawyer or that you would be given an explanation as to why you were being detained?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: After the month or so you spent in this room, where were you transferred to next?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I was transferred across the road from the SUP to the TO building.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I just ask that the witness be shown picture 50 from the Prosecution Exhibit 14. And perhaps just for the usher's sake, you could also provide photographs 4 and 5, for a matter of convenience. Could the usher please place, yes, number 50 on the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, is the building depicted in the picture there the TO building which you speak about?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And it was across the road here that you were transferred from the SUP?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher -- could you please put photograph 5 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the doors depicted in the photograph in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: This big door was the door of the room we were locked in, and the small door led to a room where 30 or 40 people had already been detained. That's where we were transferred, and this one had been closed until then.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So the door on the right-hand side, beside what looks like a van with a red cross on it, is the cellar in which you were kept; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with those photographs. Perhaps you could just leave them near the witness, and I may ask him to refer to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, how many of you were kept in that room?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: In this TO room, there was about 180 of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So there were more than just the people who were transferred with you from your particular room in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were all 180 either of Muslim or Croat ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Amongst them was there anybody wearing a military uniform or any sort of uniform, or were they only civilians?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: They were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The other 160 or so people held with you in that room, did they look to you as if they had been beaten and ill-treated in a way that you and your co-detainees obviously had?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Whilst you were detained in this room, this cell in the TO building, how often were you provided with food or sustenance?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: When we moved to the TO, we got food once a day. We got a slice or two of bread covered with either lard or with jam, and also --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I lost the second half of the translation. I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear. Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, the interpreters didn't catch all your answer, so could you please explain to us what exactly it was you were given to eat again.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: We got only one meal, in the mornings: two slices of bread with either lard or jam, and also a small glass of tea.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Being a Muslim, would you normally eat lard?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did all 180 of you have to sleep in this room behind the door we saw?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was it big enough for you all to lie down and sleep comfortably?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No. There were racks from ammunition cases. It was very crowded. And we only had one blanket underneath us. Some had to sleep on the concrete.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So do I understand that some people slept on the floor, some people tried to sleep on these racks you speak of?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And you said you had one blanket underneath you. Was that the total sleeping equipment, so to speak, that you were given by the authorities?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: How about hygiene facilities? Did you have access to toilets when you needed it?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Would you be allowed to go to toilets at specific times?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: How would you then manage to get to the toilet?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: We went also in the morning, one by one, and we had to go through the duty room where the soldier was, then through the hall, and then to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, usher. Could I ask you for your assistance just to put photo 4 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, am I correct in saying that the opening to the right of that picture leads into the toilet?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So what you've just described, having to go in through there, through the duty room and that, that's where you would have to go, is it?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And would you sometimes be beaten on your way there and back to the toilet?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Now, again perhaps just leave the photograph beside the witness, but I'm finished with it for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, maybe the witness could tell us what would happen or what happened if somebody requested to go to the toilets other than that first visit in the morning. What happened to the person?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, I think Her Honour's question is clear.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Every new request to go to the toilet would cause beatings. Because of that reason, we never requested to go to the toilet. We took it as long as we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Would this sometimes mean that people had to go to the toilet other than in the toilet; so sometimes in the cell where you were all being kept?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In this room that we were in, there were steps to go to the attic. And in this attic, we opened the door -- because they were closed. These were iron doors. And upstairs we found an old uniform. It was a green/grey uniform of the JNA. And we would go upstairs to go to the toilet, if we were talking about bowel movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Whilst you were in the TO, were you ever able to get visits from your family or relatives?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Visits were not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: On occasion, did relatives or family manage to get through bread or some clothes through -- through guards to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: But official visits were prohibited; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Is that official visits were prohibited or official visits were not prohibited?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not prohibited -- no, they were prohibited.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Mehinovic, can you estimate how long you were detained in the Territorial Defence building?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately up to September, October. At that time we were transferred by buses to the Batkovic camp. And at the TO, we were called one by one. Our eyes were bound, and we were taken to the buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So Mr. Mehinovic, I estimate that if you were kept in the SUP for a month or so, that it must have been, say, end of June, beginning of July when you were transferred to the TO, and then you stayed there for, I guess, up to four months. Is that a correct interpretation of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: During these four months in the TO, were you subjected to a variety of beatings similar to those that you had endured in the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was this just for you, or was it something that the other detainees with you also suffered?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: We all suffered.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you ever subjected to such games as Russian roulette?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you just describe how this game of Russian roulette would play out in the territorial building.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Seven or eight or ten of us would be taken out, and we would be put into a circle. And Batan Vukovic would then turn the barrel on his gun. And wherever -- no, he would turn his --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter correction.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: He would -- he would turn the barrel of his gun so that he would know where the bullet was. And wherever it was, and if -- and if -- and he would start shooting prisoners. And if the bullet was there, that person would fall. If not, then he would start shooting -- he would continue shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And was anyone ever killed during these games?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Not in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, could we clarify who the person was who was firing the gun, because I think on page 63, line 25 it's missing. Presumably it will be put in later with the audiotapes. But I'd be interested in hearing the name right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. Sorry, I didn't realise it was missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The transcript hasn't caught the name of the person who used to play Russian roulette with the barrel. Could you just repeat it again slowly for us so it's clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Nikola Vukovic, called Batan.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And Mr. Mehinovic, while this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, just a technical question. When we are talking about playing Russian roulette, we usually mean a revolver with six bullets and then turning it. And there is only one bullet in the revolver, and then you turn it around and then you, so to say, fire it. And if there is an empty place with no bullet, then it will happen. But you have always been speaking about pistols, and a pistol is something quite different compared with A revolver, because in a pistol you have a magazine with one or more bullets in it. So what are you talking about now when you are talking about playing Russian roulette? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. You are right. I think that in my previous testimony when I talked about Batan, I already emphasised that he had a revolver, and I failed to specify it right now. But I did mean his revolver, not pistol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, you said that no one was ever killed in front of you as a result of these games. But every time you were forced to play it, were you afraid that someone would be killed or that even you yourself would be killed?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Whilst you were held in the TO, did you know someone called Slobodan Jacimovic?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Jacimovic. Jacimovic. He called himself the Serbian inspector. On more than one occasion and in more than one moment, he personally called upon me and he would beat me; the reason I still have not found out. The first time I ever saw him was at the TO building. Before that, I had never heard of him or known him.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And therefore, did you learn his name from him or from other persons?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: From other people after I left the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: What sort of beatings would he inflict upon you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: He would bind me to the window of the TO building that had bars. He would beat me with the handle of -- a wooden handle of a mop. He would beat me until I was completely exhausted. And then I had to get up and lift my soles towards the -- towards the skies, and then he would hit me all over my soles.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I ask if just the usher can -- just to put picture number 4 back on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, on the right-hand side of that photograph, we can see a window with some grating. Is that the window you refer to in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the window.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And again, I'm finished with that photograph. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, I don't want to go into everything you endured during these four months in the TO. But beyond what you've described to us - the Russian roulette, particular beatings by Mr. Jacimovic - did you also have other -- regular routine beatings that would go on throughout these four months?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't quite regular, because when you were called up only -- for example, Jacimovic beat me -- if I would say that I was already beaten, he would -- I would have to lift my shirt to show that I was already beaten. And if my wounds were -- it was -- if it was visible from my wounds that I had just been beaten, then he would leave it. But if it was not, then he would beat me again.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, did any of the guards or persons who -- persons who used to have access to the TO building ever refuse to, you know, participate in hitting prisoners? Were there some good people who didn't participate?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were Zoran Jovanovic, Ranko Tinin, Djoko Pejcic from Crkvina, called Unprofor. Those were the people that never allowed while they were there to be beating, while they were on duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mehinovic, during your stay in the TO, did Mr. Miroslav Tadic ever visit the TO?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And do you know why he would come to the TO?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of exchange, when he had to come and get people, that's when he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And Mr. Tadic, would he just stand outside the yard of the TO or would he actually come into the cell where the 180 of you or so were being held?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: He would come to the yard. He would not go to the cell. He was at the door. When he'd read somebody's name, that person would go out and wait to enter the bus for the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: During your four-month period, how many times did you see Mr. Tadic come to the TO in this manner?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Personally, I only saw him once at the TO building.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you tell us, from what you saw there, what the prisoners would have looked like when Mr. Tadic came to collect them for exchange?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Every person was very happy because they were going to be exchanged. Everybody couldn't wait to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Why exactly were people so happy to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Because they would get rid of the beatings. Then nobody else would beat them. They would be free. And they would also not be in the confined space any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So in your experience, people wanted to be exchanged to avoid beatings and to escape confinement; was that it?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: These prisoners, could you describe to us what they would have looked like in terms of any visible injuries, if they had any, would they have lost any weight, what was their clothing like?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Everybody has lost weight, up to the last person. Nobody weighed the same as they did at the beginning. If they weighed a hundred kilos, during the time of exchange they would have weighed 60 to 70 kilos. We weren't receiving food. We weren't receiving quality food. The person that loses weight, it is well known that the eyes in that case become much deeper. They sink deeper into the skull. And the face changes dramatically.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did the majority of -- or indeed all the prisoners have visible bruises or wounds to their bodies?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Not everybody did. I could say, for example, Kemal Bobic, who was hit between the scalp and the left eyebrow, that part of his face was swollen, but after a while this part started rotting. There was another man. I know his last name was Galic. His entire scalp was removed. It was hanging. After a while it -- also because of festering. He was taken to Brcko to have his wound disinfected and his head bandaged up.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And did many of the detainees have the same clothes on them that they had been wearing for a long time while they were in detention?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. Do you mean the same clothing that they were wearing before?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I just want to get a picture whether these prisoners who were being taken out by Mr. Tadic for exchange would have been, for example, wearing fresh clothing, looking healthy, or whether or not they would have clothes they had been wearing in detention, maybe bloodstained from some of the beatings you described. I'm just trying to get a visual image of what the prisoners looked like at the time Mr. Tadic made his visits.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I personally don't know if they received or changed clothes, but from the TO they left -- they went out wearing the same clothes that they had when they first arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mehinovic, whilst you were for four months in the TO, did you ever receive a visit from the International Red Cross in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to whether or not the International Red Cross tried to visit you detainees in the Territorial Defence building?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Mr. Esref Zaimbegovic has informed me of that. He was taken to the TO room, where there was a guard, he and another person, and the rest of us were locked and we were threatened that not even a fly should be heard. After Esref returned, he said that the International Red Cross had been there, but only two of them were shown to the IRC, and they were told that only prisoners were there in these rooms that had quite normal conditions around them.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do just want to follow up one or two questions. I don't know whether you would like me to finish this line of questioning and then break, or save the follow-up questions for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe we can break until 1805.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And Your Honours, may I also raise one thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The Defence last month had given us a number of documents pertaining to this witness. Due to a clerical error, and no error on the part of the Defence, only one part of a document which purports to be a statement made by Mr. Mehinovic in detention came through to us. Therefore, I didn't until now have a chance to see the full statement, and I'm wondering if the Bench would indulge me just to approach the witness just on this single document. I've discussed it with my colleagues, and certainly Mr. Lukic, whose document it was, has no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Then you may discuss the document with the witness during the break. We shall resume at 1805 hours. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I just ask the usher's assistance. I've had placed on the ELMO photograph number 50. It's just a little bit out of focus at the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, perhaps again with the aid of the pointer. You just told us that a Mr. Esref Zaimbegovic was taken away into the TO building and put into a clean dormitory. If it's possible from the photograph in front of you, could you just try to demonstrate to us where he was taken to be shown to the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know firsthand which room he was in. I just know that he had been there, because when he returned to our room where we were locked up, he told me the whole story, where he had been and what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And according to that story that he told you, which building did you understand him to have been taken to?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: This one, the TO building.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Esref Zaimbegovic originally detained with you in the cell of 180 people?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I have no direct knowledge about when he was brought in. I just know that he was brought to our room where 180 of us were kept, and that's where we met.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. So he was taken -- he was with you in your room. He was taken from your room and to the building you indicated in the photograph. And that's where the ICRC saw him. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'm finished with the photograph 50 for the moment again.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, you stated that so far in the SUP building you had never been asked to give a statement. Finally during your detention in the TO building, were you brought in for interrogation and requested to make a statement?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Where were you taken to make that statement?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I was taken to the police station to the second floor, the office of Milos Savic, inspector.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you know who Milos Savic was before you saw him this time in the office?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I knew him very slightly, because even before the war he worked in the crime investigation department.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Savic wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: He was then dressed in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That day he was in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you tell whether he was armed?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No. I couldn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was he alone in the room or were there more persons apart from Mr. Milos Savic there?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: He was alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can you recall roughly how long after you had been transferred to the TO that you were called to make this statement?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure any longer. I think it was in the month of July, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And by the time you went to see Mr. Milo Savic, did you -- was your finger already broken?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And you had already sustained over a month or so of regular beatings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: From what you knew of the injuries you had sustained up until that time, would the -- were the injuries visible when you entered the room of Mr. Savic?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, the only thing you could see was the index finger.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can you recall: Were you in the same clothes that you had been arrested in on the 27th of May?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Only after the interrogation did we begin to get a change of clothes and other things that our families managed to get through to us. The guard on duty would call you into a room and give you the change of clothes, tell you to undress and put on the new clothes, and hand over the old ones to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And so that only began in the latter months of your detention; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you went up to Mr. Savic's office, did he explain to you the reasons for your detention?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No. He kept asking the same question: Where I was and where I moved in the morning of the 17th of April, 1992. To that, I had to describe all my movements in that period, where I was, in detail, throughout that day. I gave him my statement, in which I said that at 8.00, 8.30, I left my home, and seeing a group of armed people coming from the direction of the retirees' home, including Ibela Salkic, Muhamed and Hasan Bicic, and another ten or so men whose names I don't recall any longer, I stopped, because I know Ibrahim Salkic, also known as Ibela, very well. I asked him what was going on, and he told me that there was a massacre and murders going on in Donja Mahala against our people. As we went on, we passed by the department store, through Stjepan Radic Street, when we reached the Lav restaurant, and there we ran into Darko Dujmusic. Darko Dujmusic tried to talk all of us into going back home lest we die for no reason at all. We didn't waste much time talking. We returned to our homes, retracing our steps through the Stjepan Radic Street, the department store, until we reached the so-called Carrington building. In the yard of that building, we saw Muhamed, nicknamed Biber, who had come out of the building and talked to Salkic. Salkic had a walkie-talkie in his hand. The two of them went back to Muhamed's flat, and after a while they came back, whereupon Mr. Salkic informed us that there would be no problem, that he had personally talked to Nikolic. I can't remember exactly whether he was a colonel or a lieutenant colonel. Anyway, he said that he would come with his troops to Samac and that we should go home and that there would be no problem at all. We would be safe. From that yard in Djure Djakovica Street, not from my house, Mr. Kemal Atic, nicknamed Kilo, and I, set off towards the retirees club, and that is near the intersection near my house. We stood outside the retirement home for a while. There were several young men: Sladjan Grbic, Ibrahim Doslic, a former policeman in Bosanski Samac, and I think Savic was there as well, because he was from the same building. And we were discussing what was going on. Ibrahim told us, "Go home. Don't hang around here any more." My home was perhaps five minutes on foot from there. On my way, I walked Kemal Atic to his house and then returned to my home. From that moment on, I stayed in my apartment and I knew nothing of what was going on outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So Mr. Mehinovic, I take it you gave Mr. Savic a very full and detailed description of your movements on the morning of the 17th of April. Is that basically accurate?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: At any stage, did you tell him that you were carrying a weapon?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No. What I have just said is precisely what I said in my statement from the very first day.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And were you at any stage carrying a weapon but you just didn't bother to tell Mr. Savic?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you ever carrying a weapon to help out one of the other men that you met up with?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I ask that a statement be shown to this witness. I have a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: -- copy in B/C/S, which I suggest is put in front of the witness and perhaps on the ELMO so that the defendants also can see it. And I have translations here for the Bench and for the legal officer. I believe the Defence have this particular statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. Mr. Mehinovic, you can see a document in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher just to raise the document so that the handwritten -- no, the other way, just so the signature at the bottom is visible.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you have a look either at the screen or at the actual document to your right, Mr. Mehinovic. Mr. Mehinovic, perhaps if you turn around to your right. The document itself is on the ELMO. Does that look like your signature at the bottom right-hand corner of the document?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher to turn over the statement to the second page.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes what? Is the --

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] My signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The signature on the left-hand side of the document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, when you were in the room giving the statement to Mr. Savic, did you get a chance to -- did you sign a statement at the end of the description you'd just given him?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I signed when he said the investigation was over.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you read through the document that you signed?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No, because I wasn't allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Savic or any other person read it out to you before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, can I ask you to look at the second page of that document -- or Mr. Mehinovic, could I ask you to look at the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the translation, it's also the second page. And I just want to ask the witness about the first three sentences of that paragraph on the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, could I ask you just to read to yourself - I'll just ask you questions about this - the first three sentences of that paragraph. For the record - and you tell me if this is correct - the statement says: "Kemal Atic and I headed down Djure Djakovica Street. As he had two rifles, he asked me to carry one of them, saying he had pain in his shoulder. It was a rifle that cocks in the same way as an M-48 military rifle, and it may have been a small-caliber rifle. I carried the rifle as far as my house, where I handed it back to Kemal Atic." Have you read that part in that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can you see those sentences in the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the sentences. That's fine. But Mr. Savic was typing something that I couldn't see. I don't know whether he was typing what I was saying or something that he wanted to write.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Is it your case that you never said those words to him?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No. I did go together with Kemal; that much is true. But there was absolutely nothing they said about him handing me a rifle or anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And did Kemal Atic at any stage hand you a rifle?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, there was no reason why I should take that rifle. Everybody was disbanded. Everybody had scattered. What would I want with it?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I've finished for my purposes with that document. Perhaps it could be entered into evidence and given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The English translation will be Exhibit P54. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is there a Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: There should be a Serbo-Croat version, one given to the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It has just been handed over to me. It is P54 ter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, until you arrived here in The Hague to give your testimony, had anyone ever showed you that statement again since your time in Mr. Savic's office?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Let's be clear. Were you ever actually shown this statement whilst you were in Mr. Savic's office?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Only the signature, without reading it. He took the paper out of the typewriter and gave it to me to sign. That was the last time and the first time that I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. After you had finished your interview with Mr. Savic, were you returned to the SUP -- sorry, to the Territorial Defence building? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you ever called for any other interrogation or further criminal investigation inquiries?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So after this statement in July, you stayed in the TO building for another three months without any other investigation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Beyond your statement being given -- being taken, did anyone at any time show you any documents or any evidence as to why there may be any suspicion about you or your behaviour?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, you've testified already that at some stage you were transferred out of the territorial building, and I believe you put on the record that you were taken to a camp called Batkovici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: How many of you were taken from the Territorial Defence building and transferred to Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: All the prisoners that were at the TO building or in the SUP building, they were all transferred to Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you give us a rough number as to how many that would be?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Considering that there were exchanges and transfers, I think there might have been about 180 of us that arrived at Batkovici camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Whilst in the Batkovici camp, where were you detained?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: We were in a hangar for agricultural goods and machines.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you kept there just the people from Bosanski Samac or were there detainees from other parts of the former Yugoslavia with you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: After we arrived, we found about 20 people that were incarcerated there from Bijeljina and Janja.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Who were the persons guarding you whilst you were detained in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: The guard, the military, the Serbian military, they had the guard, and they were from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you ever visited by people from Bosanski Samac whilst you were in Batkovici camp?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Particular people had visits, those that were in mixed marriages. A person in a mixed marriage could have a visit at Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of the defendants - Mr. Simo Zaric, Mr. Miroslav Tadic, Mr. Milan Simic, or Mr. Blagoje Simic - whilst you were in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I only saw Mr. Tadic at Batkovici. The other gentlemen I did not see.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And I will return to Mr. Tadic's -- the time that you saw Mr. Tadic at Batkovici, but first let me again get a picture of what life was like at Batkovici. You were transferred there at the end of 1992, is that correct, or the final months of 1992?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: In Batkovici, were you subjected to beatings, as you had been in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you given any more food or water than you had been whilst you were detained at Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were the general sleeping and living conditions an improvement on Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Whilst you were in Batkovici, did you have to go out and perform any forced labour assignments?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: What sort of assignments did you have to perform?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: We had to work the fields; for example, the maize, wheat, also sugar beet. We also had to load and unload trucks with flour. We also went to work at the factory for animal food; to Panafleks, that made bendable pipes, where we made equipment for drying tobacco. We also went to a carpentry factory, where we loaded furniture, and unloaded flour that was coming through the UNHCR into those magasins.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Would these forms of labour be performed within the camp of Batkovici or would you be taken out of the camp to perform them?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: They were outside the camp. They were mostly in the town of Bijeljina. We were only working on the fields of maize, or we worked the sugar beet fields behind the hangar, and this was part of an agricultural plant in Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Would you be guarded by these Serbian military personnel you talked about earlier whilst you were performing these labour assignments?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any payment or compensation for the labour you performed?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The people you had been transferred with to Batkovici and the people you met there, were they all of Muslim and Croat ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you told whilst you were in Batkovici that you had to go on trial?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I did not know about the trial, nor was I told, until I received a summons. They only read my first and last name, and then the military police officer took me to the courtroom in Bijeljina. This was a larger, private house in which the courthouse was situated.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, I'd like just to back up a little bit. You were, I then understand, taken at some stage to a form of trial whilst you were detained in Batkovici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And you said you received a summons, and that was whilst you were in Batkovici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a summons. It was just -- they called me up. They called up my first and last name and said that they were looking for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And did they tell you that you were going to be taken to a trial or a court at that stage, when they called out your name?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: After entering the jeep, I was told that I'm going to the courthouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did they tell you why you were going to the courthouse?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't told why I was being taken. The police didn't know either.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Prior to being put into the jeep, the only official investigation you had been involved with since your detention on May 27th, 1992 was this time spent in Milos Savic's office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Where did the jeep take you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: It took me to Bijeljina, to a larger house. It was a private house. You could see that because of the private yard. But that's where the military court was located.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the house, were you served with any sort of charge sheet or indictment or given any form of information at all as to why you had been summoned to the courthouse?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did anyone approach you and orally advise you what was going to happen to you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did anyone come to you and tell you that you would be assigned a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: At any stage before you went into the courtroom, did you meet with a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, perhaps you could tell us what happened just after your arrival at the courthouse. Where did you go? Did you wait somewhere?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I waited in a room, a little bit bigger room. There were a couple of chairs there and there was a military police officer there.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And roughly how long did you have to wait in this room?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure. Maybe about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And then did someone come and get you to take you into another room, or what happened?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: When my name was called by the next officer, this police officer Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that brought me there, I went to a room where I had to stand in the middle of the room, and two police officers were standing on both of my sides. There were two police officers next to me, one civilian on the right, and one civilian on the left, while I was talking to the judge. The first time I talked to the judge, he asked me if I knew why I was here, and I said I didn't know. And then he said, "Well, you will." And that was the only -- that was the entire conversation that I had with the judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: After you had had this exchange of words with the judge, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: This police officer that came with me took me back to the waiting room. While we waited, I think some kind of a decision or what was going to happen next [as interpreted]. Maybe after about half an hour, maybe 15 minutes - I'm not sure - the other police officer that was in the room came out and said to the first one, "Take him to the correctional centre across the barracks in Bijeljina."

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I take you back to the room where the judge was? The judge had told you that you will know why you were here. Did the judge then take steps to inform you why you were there and what the charges against you were?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did the judge read out an indictment to you or a charge sheet?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Whilst you were in that room, was there anybody -- any other person who was pointed out to you as acting as your lawyer?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I did [as interpreted] know who or what he was. I only know how many people were there. There were two people in front of me sitting at a desk, and one of them was on the right-hand side, one of them was at the left-hand side, two civilians. And then there were two police officers, one on each one of my sides. I had no idea who these people were or what they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did the judge ask you to make a statement or answer any charges put to you?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did the judge ask any of the other persons in the room to answer on your behalf or to enter a plea or a defence on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Not in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: At any stage did the judge ask you to sign any documents?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: After you were taken out of this room, you said you were left to sit outside and then some people said that they should take you to the correctional centre. Were you told why you were being taken to the correctional centre?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you in fact taken to the correctional centre?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And how long were you detained in the correctional centre?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know precisely whether it was a month or more. This was a military prison of those that were fleeing the front lines. There were both Serbs and Muslims in this prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was this the first time since the 27th of May, 1992 that you had been imprisoned with anyone of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was this the first time since the 27th of May, 1992 that you had seen a judge or anyone in official authority who explained to you, so to speak, why you were being detained?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mehinovic, thinking back, could you try to put a date roughly when this incident in the Bijeljina courthouse happened?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: That might have been -- I think in January of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are a couple of questions on documents I would like to ask this witness about relating to the core issues here. Unfortunately the translations are not readily available. They're translations of the Defence documents which we received last month. So with your permission, I'm just going to move on and maybe at the beginning of tomorrow's session I will just come back to this topic and address the witness on it, presuming that we have the translations by then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, after you were detained in the correctional centre for a month, were you then transferred back to the bigger camp in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And was it whilst you were back there in Batkovici that you saw Mr. Miroslav Tadic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you say you think so, do you mean you think it was Miroslav Tadic you saw, or do you think it was around this time period that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in that time frame, but it was Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tadic just come to the camp, or did he actually come to the hangar where you were being detained in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: He came to the hangar in which we were detained at the camp, Batkovici. He had a list in his hands, and he was reading out names for exchange. At that time, my name was also on the list, and I personally saw how Mr. Sabah Seric explained and promised to give him money, and he gave him about 100 Deutschmarks in front of me. And after he went to the commander of the camp, to his office, he took off my name and put Mr. Sabah's name on the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So Mr. Mehinovic, just so we're very clear on this incident, I'm going to ask you to -- for some clarifications. He came into the hangar and he had a list in his hand. Who exactly was this?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This had to do with an exchange of some people from Bosanski Samac. I don't know exactly all the names. I can't remember what exactly was happening, but this was an exchange that was taking place. Around five or ten or seven people were being taken away by him. Which people were being taken at this particular time, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And the person who had his -- who had the list in his hands was Mr. Miroslav Tadic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: This is the same Miroslav Tadic who owns Cafe AS and who you had seen in the Territorial Defence building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So you said he read out names on the list. And I understand that your name was initially called out by Mr. Tadic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And did you understand that you were then going to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Then could you explain after the names were read out what you witnessed between -- I believe you said a Mr. Sabah Seric -- what you witnessed Mr. Sabah Seric doing.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: Sabah gave him -- gave him some money and asked him to be exchanged, so to be taken from Batkovici from Bosanski Samac and then after that, you would be exchanged. After that -- after a particular amount of time, he put Sabah on the list and took -- my name was no longer on the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you yourself see money exchange hands, or did you just hear that that's what had happened?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL MEHINOVIC
utterances.text: No. I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
